notes: ncert.nic.in (textbook.php and the textbook PDF/prelims files) refused automated fetching (robots.txt disallow) on 2026-10-19, so the NCERT contents pages, printed section headings and edition/reprint lines could not be read directly. Chapter titles were verified instead against other official government sources: NCERT's CIET audio-book pages (ciet.ncert.gov.in) and the Delhi Directorate of Education 2026-27 syllabus (edustud.nic.in), which prescribes NCERT books. 'verified': true means the title was seen in at least one of those sources.

CBSE does not publish its own mathematics syllabus for Grades 6-8. Its 2026-27 curriculum release (Circular Acad-14/2026) covers Classes IX-XII only, and CBSE circulars direct schools to the new NCERT textbooks. The 2026-27 prescription is therefore inferred from those circulars plus the Delhi DoE 2026-27 syllabus. No CBSE or NCERT notice found replaces or withdraws Ganita Prakash for 2026-27.

Section titles come from the subtopic lists in the Delhi DoE 2026-27 annual syllabus, not from the printed textbook. They appear to quote the textbook's section headings, but DoE may have shortened, merged or left some out (its list is 'for assessment purpose only'), and capitalisation follows DoE. Check them against the printed NCERT book before using them as exact headings.

Learning outcomes are written by the compiler from the chapter and section scope. They are not copied from NCERT's Learning Outcomes document, which was not consulted because ncert.nic.in was inaccessible.

Secondary sites (teachoo.com, edzy.ai, esaral.com, aglasem.com, collegedunia.com) were used only to locate official documents and to cross-check chapter order and titles. Nothing was taken from them as authoritative.

Grade 6: NCERT's Ganita Prakash (single volume, 10 chapters) has been the Grade 6 book since 2024-25. CBSE Circular Acad-12/2025 lists no further new Grade 6 book, and the Delhi DoE 2026-27 Grade 6 syllabus follows the same 10 chapters. Taken together, this shows the book is still prescribed in 2026-27.

Grade 6 English chapter titles come from the Delhi DoE 2026-27 syllabus (an official government source) and match NCERT's Hindi-medium CIET audio-book chapter list one-to-one. The printed English capitalisation was not checked against the NCERT PDF.
Grade 6 edition: given as 'first edition 2024' from general knowledge of the release year. The imprint or reprint line for the 2026-27 print was not seen.

Grade 6 Ch 1: DoE's subtopic list leaves out the opening section ('What is Mathematics?') that secondary sites show. It also merges 'Patterns in shapes' and 'Relation to number sequences' into one line, which is kept here as DoE wrote it.
Grade 6 Ch 3: DoE lists 'Playing with number patterns' and 'the Collatz conjecture' as separate items. Secondary sites show them as one textbook section, so they are kept as two DoE items.
Grade 6 Ch 5: the textbook's exact set of divisibility tests (which divisors) was not verified, so the outcome refers to divisibility tests in general.

Grade 6 Ch 6: DoE gives only three coarse subtopics ('Perimeter', 'Area', 'Area of a triangle'). The printed book has finer sections (e.g. perimeter of rectangle/square/triangle/regular polygons) that could not be verified officially.

Grade 6 Ch 9: DoE's subtopics ('Paper folding and cutting', 'Symmetries of a circle') differ from secondary-site topic lists (which mention 'Reflection Symmetry', 'Generating Symmetrical Shapes'). DoE's wording is kept.
In the DoE 2026-27 plan, chapters 1, 2, 3, 5 and 8 come before the mid-term and 4, 6, 7, 9 and 10 after it. This is Delhi-specific teaching order, not a CBSE term split, so 'term' is null.

sections.title: Patterns in shapes, relation to number sequences

outcomes.statement: Extend common number sequences (counting, odd, even, triangular, square, cube and powers of 2) and state the rule that generates each.

proposed.name: Relate figurate number sequences to their dot and shape pictures
proposed.why: Existing pattern competencies cover extending patterns and stating rules; none covers square/triangular/cube number sequences, their pictorial representations and the relations between them (e.g. sums of odd numbers are squares).

outcomes.statement: Draw dot or shape pictures of number sequences and explain why each picture gives the next number in the sequence.

proposed.name: Relate figurate number sequences to their dot and shape pictures
proposed.why: Existing pattern competencies cover extending patterns and stating rules; none covers square/triangular/cube number sequences, their pictorial representations and the relations between them (e.g. sums of odd numbers are squares).

outcomes.statement: Find and justify relations between sequences, for example that adding consecutive odd numbers from 1 gives square numbers, or that two consecutive triangular numbers add to a square number.

proposed.name: Relate figurate number sequences to their dot and shape pictures
proposed.why: Existing pattern competencies cover extending patterns and stating rules; none covers square/triangular/cube number sequences, their pictorial representations and the relations between them (e.g. sums of odd numbers are squares).

proposed.name: Formulate and test conjectures from number explorations
proposed.why: MATH.reasoning.counterexamples-intro (Grade 5) is about testing a given generalisation; Ganita Prakash repeatedly asks learners to generate conjectures from explorations (Kaprekar, Collatz, palindromes, consecutive sums) and test them systematically.

outcomes.statement: Count sides, corners or line segments in shape sequences (such as regular polygons or stacked squares) and link the counts to number sequences.

proposed.name: Relate figurate number sequences to their dot and shape pictures
proposed.why: Existing pattern competencies cover extending patterns and stating rules; none covers square/triangular/cube number sequences, their pictorial representations and the relations between them (e.g. sums of odd numbers are squares).

sections.title: Point, Line Segment, Line, Ray, Angle

outcomes.statement: Name and distinguish points, line segments, lines and rays using standard notation.
Treat an angle as an amount of turn between two arms, name its vertex and arms, and compare angles by superposition or rotation.
Measure a given angle and draw an angle of a given size with a protractor.
Classify angles as acute, right, obtuse, straight or reflex from their measures or drawings.

sections.title: Patterns of numbers on the number line

outcomes.statement: Reason about how numbers are arranged in a grid or row, for example filling a grid so that chosen cells are larger than all their neighbours (supercells).

proposed.name: Solve number grid puzzles such as supercells and magic squares
proposed.why: Grid-based number reasoning (supercells, magic squares, grid sums) is assessed in Number Play chapters and is not covered by any existing competency.

outcomes.statement: Explore digit-based processes (digit sums, palindromes by reversing and adding, Kaprekar's routine) and form and test conjectures about them.

proposed.name: Formulate and test conjectures from number explorations
proposed.why: MATH.reasoning.counterexamples-intro (Grade 5) is about testing a given generalisation; Ganita Prakash repeatedly asks learners to generate conjectures from explorations (Kaprekar, Collatz, palindromes, consecutive sums) and test them systematically.

outcomes.statement: Generate Collatz sequences from a starting number and describe their behaviour.

proposed.name: Formulate and test conjectures from number explorations
proposed.why: MATH.reasoning.counterexamples-intro (Grade 5) is about testing a given generalisation; Ganita Prakash repeatedly asks learners to generate conjectures from explorations (Kaprekar, Collatz, palindromes, consecutive sums) and test them systematically.

outcomes.statement: Use mental-calculation strategies and rough estimation to judge the size of quantities and results.

proposed.name: Round numbers and distinguish exact from approximate values
proposed.why: MATH.reasoning.estimate-check is about estimating and checking an answer; rounding to a given place and judging when an approximate value is appropriate is not covered.

outcomes.statement: Find and use number patterns in clocks and calendars.
Work out and explain a winning strategy for a simple two-player number game.

proposed.name: Find and justify winning strategies in simple number games
proposed.why: Analysing two-player number games for a winning strategy is a distinct reasoning skill in Grade 6 Number Play; MATH.reasoning.multi-step is about explaining a computation.

outcomes.statement: Collect data for a question and organise it with tally marks and a frequency table.
Read pictographs with a key, including partial symbols, and draw a pictograph from a table.
Read bar graphs with a scale and answer comparison questions from them.
Draw a bar graph from data, choosing a suitable scale and labelling the axes.
Judge whether a data display is clear and honest and suggest better design choices.

proposed.name: Choose, design and critique data displays and infographics
proposed.why: Ganita Prakash assesses aesthetic/misleading-display considerations and infographics; existing competencies only cover reading and drawing specific charts.

outcomes.statement: List common multiples and common factors of two numbers and use them to solve game or timing problems.

proposed.name: Find common factors, common multiples, HCF and LCM
proposed.why: MATH.number.factors-multiples covers factors/multiples of one number; MATH.number.euclid-algorithm is a Grade 10 algorithm. Middle-school HCF/LCM (including co-primes) has no competency.

outcomes.statement: Tell prime numbers from composite numbers and list primes in a range using a sieve.
Decide whether two numbers are co-prime.

proposed.name: Find common factors, common multiples, HCF and LCM
proposed.why: MATH.number.factors-multiples covers factors/multiples of one number; MATH.number.euclid-algorithm is a Grade 10 algorithm. Middle-school HCF/LCM (including co-primes) has no competency.

outcomes.statement: Write a number as a product of primes and use the factorisation to check divisibility and co-primeness.

proposed.name: Express a number as a product of primes
proposed.why: The only existing mention is inside MATH.number.euclid-algorithm (Grade 10, combined with the Euclidean algorithm); Grade 6 needs prime factorisation as a standalone skill.

outcomes.statement: Apply divisibility tests and explain from place value why they work.
Find the perimeters of rectangles, squares, triangles and regular polygons.
Find the area of rectangles and squares, and estimate the area of irregular shapes by counting squares on a grid.
Find the area of a triangle as half the area of a related rectangle.
Compare shapes with the same perimeter but different areas, and the reverse, and solve real-life perimeter and area problems.

sections.title: Fractional units as parts of a whole
Marking fraction lengths on number line

outcomes.statement: Interpret fractions as equal shares and as parts of a whole, and use fractional units to measure lengths.
Place fractions, including fractions greater than one, on a number line.
Convert between mixed fractions and improper fractions.

proposed.name: Convert between mixed and improper fractions
proposed.why: No existing fraction competency covers mixed fractions.

outcomes.statement: Make equivalent fractions and reduce a fraction to its lowest terms.
Compare and order fractions, including fractions with unlike denominators.
Add and subtract fractions with like and unlike denominators, including in word problems.

competencies.why: Adding (and subtracting) fractions with like denominators is already asked by fadd, whose competency the outcome is not mapped to.

sections.title: Exploring diagonals of rectangles and squares
Points equidistant from two given points

outcomes.statement: Use a compass and ruler to draw circles, arcs and figures made from them.
Construct squares and rectangles of given side lengths with ruler and compass.
Investigate the diagonals of rectangles and squares (equal length, bisecting each other, angles formed) and use them in constructions.
Locate points that are the same distance from two given points.
Find all lines of symmetry of a figure, including by folding and cutting paper.
Complete or create a figure so that it has a given line of symmetry.
Find the angles of rotational symmetry and the order of rotational symmetry of a figure.

proposed.name: Find the order and angles of rotational symmetry
proposed.why: Existing symmetry competencies (symmetry-fold, symmetry-lines) cover reflection symmetry only.

outcomes.statement: Describe the reflection and rotational symmetries of circles and regular polygons.

proposed.name: Find the order and angles of rotational symmetry
proposed.why: Existing symmetry competencies (symmetry-fold, symmetry-lines) cover reflection symmetry only.

outcomes.statement: Represent positive and negative integers on a number line (for example floors above and below ground) and order them.
Add and subtract integers using a token (positive/negative counter) model and the number line.
Solve problems involving integers in contexts such as bank balances, temperature and height above or below sea level.
Complete integer grid puzzles (e.g. grids with equal row and column sums) and explain the reasoning.
